find: The exam will not ask you about your trip directly, but it will give you an unfamiliar fieldwork scenario in a UK river or coastal landscape and ask you to design, carry out, present or evaluate the kind of investigation you actually did. Examiners expect you to write about
replace: The exam asks about your own fieldwork and also sets an unfamiliar fieldwork scenario in a UK river or coastal landscape, so you must be able to design, carry out, present or evaluate that kind of investigation. Write about
note: F1: Paper 3 Sections A and B do assess the student's own investigations, so 'the exam will not ask you about your trip' is wrong and contradicts the next clause.

find: Whatever you choose, write the reason in your method — examiners reward justified choices.
replace: Whatever you choose, write the reason in your method.

replace: You may be asked how risks were managed. A specific answer, such as ‘we checked the Environment Agency river-level gauge that morning’, is worth far more than ‘we were careful’.
note: F2: invented mark-scheme claim (score zero / score full marks).

find: Random sampling means stopping every fifth passer-by; systematic sampling means standing at fixed sites;
replace: Random sampling means choosing people by chance, so everyone has the same chance of being asked; systematic sampling means using a fixed rule, such as stopping every fifth passer-by or surveying at set sites;
note: F3: random and systematic are swapped. Stopping every fifth person is systematic sampling. This contradicts the spec's 'systematic vs random vs stratified' and lesson 1's own definition.

find: Examiners reward students who name a fix, not just complain about bias.
replace: Name a fix in your evaluation rather than only pointing out the bias.
note: F4: invented examiner claim.

find: Naming a specific fix in the exam scores higher than complaining about bias.
replace: In the exam, name a specific fix rather than only pointing out the bias.
note: F4: invented mark claim.

find: Examiners use the formula TEA: Trend, Examples, Anomalies.
replace: A useful structure is TEA: Trend, Examples, Anomalies.
note: F5: TEA is a teaching mnemonic, not an examiner formula.

find: Vague comments (‘the data was not very reliable’) score nothing without a reason and a fix.
replace: Vague comments such as ‘the data was not very reliable’ are worth little without a reason and a fix.
note: F5: invented mark claim.

find: For describe questions, examiners watch for at least two pieces of data and one anomaly — if you don’t reference figures, the maximum is half marks.
replace: For describe questions, give at least two pieces of data and one anomaly; an answer with no figures stays in the lower bands.
note: F5: invented mark-scheme rule ('the maximum is half marks').

find: The UK’s population reached around 68 million in 2025 and is forecast to pass 73 million by 2050, driven mainly by net migration of around 300,000 a year and slowly rising life expectancy.
replace: The UK’s population passed 69 million in 2024 and is projected to reach 72.5 million by 2032 and 76.6 million by 2047, driven mainly by net migration and slowly rising life expectancy.
note: F6: ONS mid-2024 estimate is 69.3 million, and the 2022-based projections reach 72.5 million by mid-2032 and 76.6 million by mid-2047 - not 73 million by 2050.

note: F6/F7: projection corrected, and 500 m3 of water per person is ten times too high - UK domestic use averages about 150 litres a day, roughly 55 m3 a year.
